extracted.intended_audience: founders of bootstrapped startups and startup marketers considering press/PR
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for when and how bootstrapped startup founders should pursue press, how to pitch reporters, develop a founder voice, and avoid common PR mistakes. Emphasizes earned media and audience-building over agency-driven PR before product-market fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure press by business outcomes, not vanity metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Press coverage should be evaluated by whether it moves key business metrics (customers, revenue), not by vanity metrics like number of articles or impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most coverage doesn't move the customer needle; pickup measured in inbound is often disappointing. Prefer ROI-focused channels (direct customer outreach, audience building such as newsletter/podcast/social) over chasing coverage for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue press only for high-impact business events
rubrics_metrics.description: Press is worth pursuing when tied to significant business events that justify the effort because they impact valuation, hiring, or brand positioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: major capital raise, hiring/recruiting acceleration needed, acquisition/exit positioning, crisis you must respond to, and long-term brand building over years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build an owned audience before relying on press
rubrics_metrics.description: Have an audience (newsletter, social followers) in place before expecting press to drive meaningful outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hustle built audience organically through its newsletter; press largely came because of that audience rather than the other way around. Audience-building provides more reliable ROI than press alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Founder voice as the brand
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the founder's voice publicly as a central element of the company's brand and media presence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam's founder voice was The Hustle's brand — being quotable and memorable helped secure coverage. Work on being a clear, authentic, and repeatable voice that reporters and audiences remember.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay hiring a PR firm until you have scale (≈>$5M ARR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't invest heavily in PR agencies before you have demonstrated scale and product-market fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hustle didn't hire a PR firm until after $5M+ ARR. Common mistake: spending too much on PR before product-market fit or traction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earn coverage through interesting, useful content
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage is more likely when you create content that is counter-intuitive, share-worthy, or positions the company as a media property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What got The Hustle coverage: counter-intuitive market analysis, funny/share-worthy newsletter content, and building The Hustle as a media property rather than a generic startup. Being interesting often earns coverage without paid PR outreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have counter-intuitive or contrarian analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce insights that challenge expectations and offer a fresh perspective on markets or trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counter-intuitive market analysis was explicitly noted as a driver of coverage — these types of ideas are more likely to get reporter interest and shares.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create funny, share-worthy newsletter content
rubrics_metrics.description: Make content that people want to forward or discuss; humor and shareability increase pickup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hustle's shareable newsletter material helped attract press; invest in content craft that encourages organic sharing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Position the company as a media property
rubrics_metrics.description: Build your brand with media sensibilities — treat your offering as content-first where appropriate, not just a product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Hustle was built as a media property, which made press coverage more natural and valuable; this is a strategic choice that changes how reporters perceive you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be quotable and memorable as a founder
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop phrases, narratives, or viewpoints that reporters can easily quote and attribute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam being a quotable, memorable founder directly led to more coverage. Practice clear, concise, and opinionated soundbites in industry conversations.

rubrics_metrics.name: One reporter at a time (pitching rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When reaching out, target a single reporter per outreach rather than blasting many at once.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam's rule: One reporter at a time. This supports personalization and reduces the chance of misfires or public embarrassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read multiple past articles before pitching a reporter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do research: read about five articles by a reporter before pitching them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding a reporter’s beat and style enables personalization and increases the likelihood your pitch resonates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a specific subject line
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft a subject line that clearly signals relevance; avoid vague or generic subject lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subject line must be specific — this helps the reporter quickly judge whether to open the pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep pitch body under 150 words
rubrics_metrics.description: Make pitches short and to the point; limit the body of the email to 150 words or fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise pitches respect reporters' time and force you to communicate the news hook succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always include a phone number in the pitch
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide direct contact information so reporters can easily reach you for follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam's rule: phone number always included — reduces friction for quick clarifications and follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow up once, then drop it
rubrics_metrics.description: Send a single follow-up if you don't get a response, then cease outreach for that story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive follow-ups are detrimental; one polite follow-up is acceptable, then move on to other reporters or stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tweet substantively in your space
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Twitter/X to offer meaningful commentary and insights in your domain as part of founder voice development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive tweets help you build visibility, credibility, and quotable lines that reporters notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build a newsletter or blog of your own
rubrics_metrics.description: Create owned content channels (newsletter, blog) to cultivate an audience and demonstrate thought leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owned channels were crucial to The Hustle’s growth and press success; they provide a steady way to test ideas and create shareable content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have opinions, not just announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Public communications should express viewpoints and insights, rather than only broadcasting product updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opinions make you interesting and quotable; announcements without substance are ignored by reporters and audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate relationships before you need them
rubrics_metrics.description: Build long-term relationships with reporters and industry figures ahead of major press needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam emphasizes long-term relationship building — cultivating rapport early increases the chance reporters will cover you when important events occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid spending on PR before product-market fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invest heavily in PR services before you have product-market fit and demonstrable traction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common mistake: spending too much on PR firms early. This is inefficient relative to building product, customers, and owned audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't rely on wire-only distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the belief that press release wire distribution alone will generate effective coverage or results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wire-only distribution thinking it'll work is listed as a common mistake — earned, personalized outreach and owned audience-building are more effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Look at me" announcements are ineffective
rubrics_metrics.description: Announcements that exist solely to attract attention without substantive news value are unlikely to generate meaningful press or business outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam warns against 'look at me' announcements with no substance; press should be tied to something newsworthy or useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Never burn an embargo
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect reporter embargoes; violating them can severely damage relationships and future coverage prospects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burning an embargo is cited as a 'career-ending mistake' — treat embargoes seriously to maintain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and accuracy as competitive advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: Be truthful with numbers and claims; honesty builds trust and protects reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lying or exaggerating numbers 'catches up' — honesty is listed both as a core quality rubric item and as a competitive advantage over dishonest peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personalize pitches
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor outreach to the specific reporter and story; personalization is a basic quality metric for pitching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality rubric lists 'personalized pitches'; connected practices include reading a reporter’s work, specific subject lines, and concise, relevant bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive news worth telling
rubrics_metrics.description: Only pitch or seek coverage when there is genuinely newsworthy, substantive content or developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality rubric: 'substantive news worth telling' — this echoes multiple anti-patterns (avoid announcements without substance) and is foundational to effective press.
